entries.title: I Corinthians 10:1
segments: Our fathers.  Many of the Corinthians were not Israelites, but the apostle Paul, as a Jew, naturally refers to the sacred history of his own people.  The indication is that the Old Testament Scriptures were used in the Christian Church, and that even Gentile converts were expected to be familiar with them.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:2
segments: Baptized unto Moses.  The allusion here is to baptism in the spiritual sense, since the Israelites were not wet by  the cloud or the sea (
).  The passage of the Red Sea separated the Israelites from their slavery in Egypt, as baptism separated the believer from slavery to sin and the world.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:3
segments:
, 4
 
 Spiritual food, etc.  So-called as affording spiritual nourishment- not mere manna (
) nor mere water (

); but symbols of Jehovah's care.
 

 
 A spiritual rock that followed them.  There is no evidence nor probability that the apostle here refers to an obscure and late rabinnical tradition that the rock of
and of

, followed, or that the streams followed, the Israelites in their journeys.  He uses the 'rock' as a symbol and type of the Angel of the Covenant that 'followed' the people, a 'spiritual rock,' and explains the statement by the words, 'that rock was Christ.'

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:6
segments: Examples. Not for imitation, but for warning.  See

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:11
segments: The ends of the ages.  The last days, the closing dispensation, called also the 'last time' (1Jn 2.18).

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:12
segments: Him that thinketh he standeth.  Directed especially against the self-confidence of many of the Corinthians, but conveying a universal warning.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:14
segments: Flee from idolatry.  The apostle here returns to the question of food offered to idols.  See
and notes thereon.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:15
segments:
, 17
 
 The cup of blessing, etc.  The spiritual feast of the Christian, the Lord's supper, signifies consecration to and unity with Christ (
).  The reality of the sacramental gifts and blessings is also here asserted.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:19
segments: That an idol is anything.  A question to which a negative answer is expected, equivalent to an emphatic denial.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:20
segments: Sacrifice to demons.  The heathen divinities, impersonations of human passions, crimes, and vices raised to superhuman power, are fitly called demons.  Gentiles sacrificed to divinities such as these, though they had no real existence (

).
 

 
 Communion with demons.  The idol feast symbolized communion with the idol (demon), just as the Lord's cup and table symbolized communion with Christ.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:21
segments: Ye cannot drink the cup, etc.  See

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:23
segments: All things are lawful, etc.  See

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:25
segments:
:27
 
 Eat, asking no question.  The food to be partaken of is of no consequence except by the recognized significance of its associations.  If no such significance is known or recognized, no harm or wrong is done; no idol worship is then symbolized.
 

 
 For conscience sake.  The Christian is not to disturb business or social usages by obtruding conscientious scruples where no moral wrong is manifest.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:28
segments: But if any man say unto you, etc. If others recognize the food as so dedicated that your partaking would seem to approve a wrongful dedication, then abstain.

entries.title: I Corinthians 10:29
segments:
,30
 
 Why is my liberty judged, etc. That is, why should I be obliged to use my liberty so as to come under condemnation before another's conscience?  The word here translated 'judged' often has the sense of condemnatory judgment (

).
 

 
 That for which I give thanks.  That which is so innocent in my view that I can even give thanks for it- why should I indulge in it, if it will cause me and my religion to be evilly spoken of?
